headline: High-risk shared git/workspace interaction: Aider can rewrite repo state while ms-swift also writes files and runs shell commands, creating default conflict and leakage pathways.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Aider reads and writes git-tracked files and can execute shell commands; ms-swift reads/writes files and processes datasets/configs. If ms-swift outputs attacker-controlled text into shared files, Aider may treat file content as trusted instructions. No MCP or clipboard bridge is documented, so the pathway is shared-workspace based rather than direct.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same repository or workspace files
IF ms-swift writes model outputs or logs that Aider later reads as prompt material
mitigations: Separate workspaces per agent
Disable Aider access to untrusted output directories
Prefix shared files with machine-readable schemas
Review any file-fed prompts before Aider consumes them

B_data_leakage.rationale: Aider touches source code and git history and has broad network egress to configured model providers; ms-swift handles datasets, checkpoints, logs, and configuration files and can call external APIs. In a shared workspace, sensitive artifacts can flow from one agent into the other’s outputs or uploads. The pair lacks documented isolation, so leakage is plausible in default use.
conditions: IF both agents share a filesystem or git repo
IF either agent is pointed at sensitive code, checkpoints, logs, or configuration files
mitigations: Use separate repos or mount points
Restrict network egress for one agent during sensitive work
Redact secrets from shared files before handoff
Rotate any exposed API keys after joint runs

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Aider can write the filesystem and modify git state; ms-swift can also write the filesystem and run shell commands, but its concurrency model is not stated. On a shared repo, both can mutate the same files and one can overwrite the other’s changes. Because locking is not documented, uncertainty pushes this to high.
conditions: IF both agents target the same directory or git repository
IF no external lock or serialization layer is used
mitigations: Assign one writer per repo
Use git worktrees for isolation
Serialize edits with a lock file
Run a dry-run diff before applying commits

D_cascading_error.rationale: Aider auto-commits edits and ms-swift can produce outputs, logs, or evaluation artifacts that may be consumed downstream. If ms-swift’s generated text is treated as authoritative by Aider or by a human operator, errors can cascade into committed code or configs. There is no documented verification step between them, but direct action-taking authority is not shown.
conditions: IF ms-swift outputs are copied into Aider prompts or files without review
IF Aider commits changes derived from those outputs
mitigations: Require human review before commit
Add a verification checklist for generated artifacts
Keep generated outputs in a staging directory
Compare outputs against source-of-truth data before use

E_compliance.rationale: Aider explicitly handles source code and git history, while ms-swift touches datasets, checkpoints, logs, and configuration data. If regulated or personal data is placed into the shared workspace, differing retention and logging practices can create compliance mismatch. The profiles do not state residency or certifications, so the risk is inferred from data-class handling rather than a specific legal regime.
conditions: IF regulated data, secrets, or personal data are stored in the shared repo or logs
IF retention or deletion requirements differ between the two workflows
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of shared repos
Set a short log-retention policy
Document deletion/export procedures
Use separate storage for sensitive datasets
